title: Reversible and Irreversible Changes
seo_title: Year 6 Science: Reversible and Irreversible Changes Worksheets (Australian Curriculum)
standard_text: Compare reversible changes, including dissolving and changes of state, and irreversible changes, including cooking, burning and rusting, that produce new substances (summary of the Australian Curriculum v9.0 Science content description).
meta_desc: Free Year 6 science worksheets on reversible and irreversible changes: melting, dissolving and evaporating, burning, cooking and rusting, and the signs of a new substance. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Reversible changes can be undone; irreversible changes make new materials.
body_html:
How to think about it

Ask: can the change be undone, and is a new material made?

  • Reversible: melting, freezing, evaporating, condensing and dissolving. The material can be got back.
  • Irreversible: burning, cooking, rusting and rotting. New materials are made and the change cannot be undone.
  • Signs of a new material: gas bubbles, a new smell, light, heat given off or taken in, or a lasting colour change.
Example

Salt dissolves in water. Reversible?

evaporate the water

the salt is left

Answer: yes

Example

Damper bakes in hot coals. Reversible?

the dough turns into new materials

Answer: no

Common mistakes

  • Thinking dissolved salt or sugar has disappeared.
  • Calling melting irreversible because it takes time to undo.
  • Thinking every colour change makes a new material (mixing paints does not).

faq.a: Yes. When sugar or salt dissolves, it spreads through the water. If the water evaporates, the sugar or salt is left behind.
Burning makes new materials such as ash, smoke, carbon dioxide and water vapour. These cannot be turned back into the wood or paper.

faq.q: What are signs of a chemical (irreversible) change?
faq.a: Look for gas bubbles, a new smell, light, heat being given off or taken in, or a colour change that does not go back.

items.e: Changes of state, dissolving and mixing can be reversed.

it is only a change of state

items.q: Which change is irreversible?

items.q: When a candle burns, which part of the change is reversible?

items.q: Why does a rusty bike chain not turn back into shiny steel?
c: Rust melts when it is cold.
It can be scrubbed back into iron easily.
Rust is a new material made from iron, water and oxygen.
items.e: Rusting is irreversible.

items.q: Which is a physical change?

items.e: Water boiling in a pot does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Which change makes a new material: freezing orange juice into icy poles, melting candle wax, melting chocolate or plaster of Paris setting?

items.e: Burning, cooking, rusting and fizzing reactions make new materials.

items.q: Which is a physical change?

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material has been made: the change cannot be undone, the material changes shape, the material dissolves and disappears from view or the material gets colder?
c: the material dissolves and disappears from view
items.e: Gas, colour change, heat and light are signs of an irreversible change.

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material may have been made?
c: bubbles of gas, a new smell or heat given off
items.e: These are signs of a chemical change.

items.q: Noah mixes hydrogen peroxide and yeast. The thermometer reads 18 °C before mixing and 27 °C one minute later. What does this temperature change suggest?
c: A new substance may have formed.
items.e: The temperature changed by 9 degrees on its own. A temperature change when substances mix is evidence of a chemical change.

items.q: Bicarb soda is added to vinegar and it fizzes. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows gas bubbles, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: A sparkler is lit and gives off bright light and sparks. What kind of change is this?
items.e: The metal powder in a sparkler burns and makes new substances, giving off light and heat.

items.q: A bubbling mixture is not always a chemical change. Which example only has a physical change?
items.e: Boiling water makes bubbles of water vapour. No new substance forms.

items.q: Kai mixes vinegar and steel wool. The thermometer reads 23 °C before mixing and 28 °C one minute later. What does this temperature change suggest?
c: A new substance may have formed.
items.e: The temperature changed by 5 degrees on its own. A temperature change when substances mix is evidence of a chemical change.

items.q: A student mixes two clear liquids, and a yellow solid appears. What is the solid?
c: a new substance made by the mixing
items.e: A new solid that forms when two liquids mix is evidence of a chemical change.

items.q: Two clear liquids are mixed and a cloudy white solid appears. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a new solid, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material has been made: the colour changes for good, the material dissolves and disappears from view, the material gets colder or the material is cut into pieces?
c: the material is cut into pieces
the material dissolves and disappears from view
items.e: Gas, colour change, heat and light are signs of an irreversible change.

items.q: Which is a sign that a new material has been made: the colour changes for good, the material changes shape, the material dissolves and disappears from view or the material gets colder?
c: the material dissolves and disappears from view
items.e: Gas, colour change, heat and light are signs of an irreversible change.

items.q: A cake batter rises and turns brown in the oven. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows gas and a new colour, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: When bicarb soda and vinegar are mixed, bubbles form. What are the bubbles?
c: air that was already in the cup
items.e: The fizzing is a new gas, carbon dioxide, made by the chemical change.

items.q: Milk left out for days smells sour. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a new smell, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: A nail left outside turns red-brown and flaky. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
c: a new colour and a new solid
items.e: The observation shows a new colour and a new solid, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Iron rusts in wet air. Which property shows rust is a new substance?
c: Rust is red-brown and crumbles instead of being shiny and strong.
Rust is a solid, like iron.
Rust is the same colour as iron.
items.e: Rust has different properties from iron, so it is a new substance.

items.q: Salt dissolves in water. Has the salt disappeared?
c: No. It is spread through the water and can be got back by evaporation.
items.e: Dissolving is reversible.

items.q: A hand warmer pack is opened and gets hot. What evidence of a chemical change is there?
items.e: The observation shows a temperature change, which is evidence that a new substance formed.

items.q: Which change is reversible?
items.e: The water vapour can condense back into water.

items.q: Which kitchen change makes a new substance?
c: toasting bread until it turns brown
items.e: Toasting changes the bread into new brown substances with a new smell and taste.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: A puddle evaporating does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Lemonade powder is stirred into water and the water turns yellow. Is a new substance formed?
c: No. The powder dissolves and colours the water, making a mixture.
items.e: The powder only dissolves. The colour comes from the powder spreading through the water.

items.q: What is an irreversible change?
c: a change that cannot be undone and usually makes new materials
a change that can easily be undone
items.e: Burning, cooking and rusting are irreversible.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Fireworks exploding makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: What is a chemical change?
c: a change from solid to liquid
a change that makes one or more new substances
items.e: In a chemical change, the particles join in new ways to make new substances with new properties.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: A glow stick lighting up makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
c: leaves rotting in a compost pile
items.e: Dissolving sugar in tea does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Ice melts into water. Is water a new substance?
c: No. Ice and water are the same substance in different states.
Yes, because it is a liquid now.
items.e: Changing state is a physical change. Water can freeze back into the same ice.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
items.e: Breaking a glass does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Which is not a sign of a physical change?
c: a gas forming when two liquids mix
a change from liquid to gas when heated
items.e: A new gas from mixing can mean a new substance. Changing shape, size or state are physical changes.

items.q: Which word best describes what happens to particles in a chemical change?
c: They rearrange to form new substances.
items.e: No particles disappear. They join together in new ways, which makes new substances.

items.q: Salt water is heated until the water is gone and salt is left. What does this show about dissolving salt?
c: It was a physical change: the salt was still there.
items.e: The same salt comes back, so no new substance had formed.

items.q: A new substance has
c: exactly the same properties as before
different properties from the substances that formed it
items.e: Rust is red-brown and crumbly, very different from shiny, strong iron. Different properties tell you it is a new substance.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
c: water vapour condensing on a mirror
items.e: Toast browning in a toaster makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which is a physical change?
c: food being digested in your stomach
items.e: Bending a paper clip does not make a new substance. The others all make new substances.

items.q: Which is a chemical change?
items.e: Milk going sour makes a new substance. The others only change shape, size or state, or mix things.

items.q: Which needs oxygen from the air?
items.e: Both react with oxygen.

items.q: Sugar dissolves in water. Why is this a physical change?
c: The sugar is still sugar; the water can evaporate to get it back.
items.e: Dissolving makes a mixture. Evaporate the water and the sugar crystals are left behind.

items.q: Mixing blue paint and yellow paint makes green paint. What kind of change is this?
c: a chemical change, because it gives off heat
a physical change: the two paints are mixed
a chemical change, because the colour changed
items.e: The colours only blend. Not every colour change means a new substance.

items.q: Which change makes a mixture, not a new substance?
items.e: Raisins and cereal can be picked apart. Each keeps its own properties.

items.q: How are iron railings stopped from rusting?
c: painting or oiling them to keep water and air away
items.e: Barrier methods.
